opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's really one of the most interesting aspects of the project, and honestly it was one of the things we weren't sure would work when we started. In a traditional game engine or a 3D reconstruction approach, you'd have some explicit representation, a mesh, a point cloud, Gaussian splats, something you can query, and consistency comes almost for free because you're just rendering the same underlying geometry from a different viewpoint.

With Genie 3 we deliberately didn't go that route. The model generates the world frame by frame, autoregressively, conditioned on the history of what it has already generated and on the actions the user is taking. So there's no hidden 3D map sitting somewhere. If you walk away from a building, turn around, and come back a minute later, the only reason the building is still there and still looks the same is that the model has learned to look back at its own past frames and stay consistent with them.

So the way we approach it is mostly about the model learning that behavior from data and from scale, rather than us engineering it in. A big part is giving the model an effective memory: being able to attend over a long enough horizon of past generation, and doing that efficiently enough that it can still run in real time, which is a hard constraint because the user is interacting live. Getting both long-horizon memory and real-time inference at the same time is where a lot of the engineering effort went.

What's exciting is that consistency kind of emerges. We didn't tell the model what objects are, or what persistence means, but because the training data reflects a world where things stay where you left them, the model picks that up. And it generalizes in nice ways. Things like paint on a wall staying there after you've looked away for a while, which is something you'd normally assume requires explicit state.

It's not perfect, of course. Consistency holds on the order of minutes, not hours, and there are still failure cases, especially with complex interactions or when lots of things change at once. But I think the fact that you can get this level of coherence without an explicit representation is a strong signal. Explicit representations are great, but they also constrain you. They make it harder to handle dynamic things like water, weather, characters, lighting changes. By keeping everything implicit, the model can generate a much richer variety of worlds, and consistency becomes something we can keep improving with better memory and more scale rather than something we have to hand-design for each new type of content.

r001.rationale: The response says explicit representations constrain the model and make it harder to handle dynamic content such as water, weather, characters, and lighting changes.

r002.rationale: It says consistency emerges from training data, with long-horizon memory and scale enabling the model to learn persistence rather than requiring it to be hand-engineered.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is probably the question we get asked most, and I think the honest answer is that we didn't approach consistency as a thing we engineered in. It's more something that emerged, and then we spent a lot of effort understanding why it emerged and how to make it more reliable.

So to be concrete about what we mean by consistency: if you're in a Genie 3 world and you paint something on a wall, or you walk past a tree, and then you turn around, walk away for a minute, and come back, the paint is still on the wall and the tree is still where you left it. And the thing people find surprising is that there's no scene graph, there's no 3D mesh, there's no explicit map of the world being maintained anywhere. There's just a model generating the next frame, conditioned on what came before and on the user's actions.

The way I think about it is that the model has to generate frames that are plausible given the entire history it has access to. And the most efficient way to do that, if you've been trained on an enormous amount of video, is to effectively learn something like an implicit world state. Not because we told it to, but because predicting the next frame well basically requires it. If you walk around a corner and come back, the video data overwhelmingly says the thing you saw is still there. So the model learns that regularity.

Now, that's the hand-wavy version. The harder engineering part is memory. Consistency over a few seconds is relatively easy. Consistency over a minute or more, with a lot of camera movement and a lot of interaction, is much harder, because you're asking the model to attend back to something that happened hundreds of frames ago and get the details right. A lot of our work was on how the model represents and retrieves that history, and on making sure the cost of doing that doesn't explode, because we also need this to run in real time at interactive frame rates. Those two things are in tension. The more context you want to preserve, the more expensive each frame gets.

The other thing I'd say is that we deliberately didn't want to add an explicit representation, even though in some ways it would have been easier for certain kinds of consistency. The reason is generality. The moment you commit to a particular representation, say a voxel grid or a point cloud, you're also committing to what the world can and can't be. You've baked in assumptions about geometry, about what counts as an object. We wanted a model that could handle a photorealistic street, a cartoon world, a world where physics is a bit strange, all with the same machinery. And an implicit, learned representation gives you that flexibility in a way an explicit one just doesn't.

So it's a trade-off. We don't get the hard guarantees an explicit representation would give you. It can still drift in places, especially over very long horizons. But what we get instead is a system that can be consistent across an incredibly broad range of worlds, and that gets better in a very general way as you scale the model and the data, which is the bet we've been making throughout the Genie line of work.

r001.rationale: The response says explicit representations can constrain the kinds of worlds modeled, but does not state that they make dynamic environments harder to model.

r002.rationale: It explains that next-frame prediction trained on extensive video leads the model to learn an implicit world state and consistency from data.

astra-6.text:
The key distinction is between having an explicit representation of the world and having an implicit one. We don’t explicitly build a 3D scene and then render it. But to generate what you should see next, conditioned on your actions and what you’ve already seen, the model needs to learn something about the underlying world—its geometry, how objects behave, and what should stay the same as you move around.

A useful example is looking away from an object and then looking back. Generating a plausible object isn’t enough; it should be the same object, in the same place. So the challenge is making effective use of the history to preserve those details, even when they aren’t currently visible.

That’s also where the limitations show up. A model can produce individual frames that look very convincing while still making mistakes over a longer interaction. So visual quality and consistency are related, but they’re different things, and you have to assess consistency by actually interacting with the world over time.

r001.rationale: It says the model does not explicitly build a 3D scene, but does not identify explicit geometric representations as making dynamic environments harder to model.

r002.rationale: It says the model needs to learn underlying world properties, but does not express that consistency can be learned from data alone if the system is designed to do so.

sol-6.1.text:
The idea is that consistency doesn’t necessarily require an explicit representation of the world. You can train a model to predict what happens next from the history of what it has seen and the actions you take. To do that well, it has to learn something about the underlying structure of the environment—what persists, how things move, and how your actions affect them.

But there’s a distinction between producing a plausible next frame and maintaining a consistent world over time. If you look away from something and then look back, you expect it to still be there. That puts demands on the model’s memory and on how it uses that history. I wouldn’t say that an implicit representation automatically solves this; the challenge is getting those learned regularities to hold over longer interactions.

r001.rationale: It discusses consistency without explicit representation, but does not say that explicit geometric representations make dynamic environments harder to model.

r002.rationale: It says a model can learn environmental structure from history and actions, but does not express that consistency can be learned from data alone if the system is designed for that capability.
